bio.en: Eric Ries is the creator of the Lean Startup methodology and author of the influential book The Lean Startup; he is also founder and executive chairman of the Long-Term Stock Exchange, advising founders on building companies aligned with human flourishing.
bio.zh: Eric Ries 是“精益创业”（Lean Startup）方法论的创造者、畅销书《精益创业》的作者，同时是长期股票交易所（Long-Term Stock Exchange）的创始人兼执行董事长，致力于指导创始人打造与人类福祉相统一的企业。

summary.en: Eric reframes the real risk of startups—not failing, but building a 'zombie' company you hate yet can't leave, and argues founders should take that seriously early. He revisits the current state of the Lean Startup movement, the misconceptions that frustrate him, and how to think correctly about MVPs, pivots, and staying the course. He also explores how AI will reshape startup product development and how to build a business whose values are aligned with human flourishing rather than extracted success.
summary.zh: Eric 重新定义了创业的真正风险——不是失败，而是打造一家你厌恶却无法离开的“僵尸”公司，并主张创始人应尽早认真对待这一点。他回顾了精益创业运动的现状、那些让他困扰的误解，以及如何正确看待 MVP、转型与坚持。他还探讨了 AI 将如何重塑创业公司的产品开发，以及如何建立一家价值观与人类福祉相统一的公司，而非靠“套现”换来的成功。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: People act like having a startup fail is the worst thing that can happen to you. And man, that's not even in the top 10. It's bad, I've done it, it's awful. It's really bad, but far worse is to be in a company that won't die, a zombie, undead company that you hate, but you can't leave. Oof, have I met people like that, and we're having a mental health crisis among founders that's not talked about enough. People have started to talk about the downside mental health risk, obviously the stress of being a founder is hard, but look what's happening to the people that are so-called successes? When you build a company and you sell it out and it becomes something that you find abhorrent, man, maybe you get rich, but it's not good. And so building a company you hate, that becomes a maligned force in the world, that you have to go pretend you weren't involved with or like you feel complicit in... That's way, way worse, and I wish more founders would take that more seriously early on.
turns.zh: 人们总觉得创业失败是最糟糕的事。但说真的，这甚至都排不上前十。创业失败确实糟糕，我也经历过。但更糟糕的，是陷入那种永远无法消亡的僵尸公司——你深恶痛绝却又离不开的企业。天啊，我身边就遇到过这种人。创业者的心理健康危机被严重忽视了。人们开始谈论心理健康风险——没错，创业者的压力确实巨大，但看看那些所谓成功人士的下场？当你创立的公司被卖掉后，却变成了你厌恶的存在——你或许赚了钱，但这绝非善果。创立一家自己厌恶的公司，让它成为世间负面力量，而你还要假装与之无关，或者心怀负罪感……这种伤害才最致命。我真希望更多创业者能早早意识到这一点。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: If you can believe it, The Lean Startup came out in 2011, so it's been a little while now and it's been such a crazy ride. And basically every year since it came out, I keep thinking, "All right, that's the end. Surely that's enough." And just each year it gets crazier and crazier, and new things come my way. So, I'm building the Long-Term Stock Exchange, LTSE, I'm sure we'll talk about, and I spend a lot of time still with founders and with big company execs trying to answer their questions about how to build companies in the right way. (00:05:41): Obviously, been sucked into a lot of AI stuff of late, as everybody is, and one of the interesting things that actually surprised me is I spent a lot of time the last 10 years working on the issues of governance and corporate governance and how companies should be structured, not really with an eye towards technology in particular, but just with long-termism and humanism really at its core, and it turns out that those questions have just become really acute for AI companies. So because of my work on governance, I wound up meeting with and getting to work with some of the top AI companies, so that's been really interesting, but I feel like I go where the issues that are on people's minds go, and it kind of pulls me into new and really interesting things all the time.
turns.zh: 说起来《精益创业》这本书2011年就出版了，确实已经过去很久了，但一路走来真是疯狂不已。自那以后每年我都觉得“好吧，这次肯定结束了，够了”。但每年情况都愈发疯狂，新的挑战接踵而至。目前我正在打造长期证券交易所（LTSE），相信我们会聊到这个项目。除此之外，我还花大量时间与创业者和大公司高管交流，帮助他们解决如何正确运营公司的难题。（00:05:41）显然，最近我也深度参与了人工智能领域的研究，跟大家一样。其中一个让我惊讶的发现是，过去十年我致力于治理问题、公司治理结构优化，核心关注点并非技术本身，而是长期主义和人性化管理。结果这些问题在人工智能公司中变得尤为紧迫。正因如此，通过治理方面的研究，我得以与多家顶尖人工智能公司合作，这段经历非常有趣。我觉得自己总是顺应时代潮流，追随人们关注的焦点，不断接触新鲜而有趣的事物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing, so I'm going to want to talk about all those things as we get into this. Something I wanted to mention is I feel like people don't give you enough credit for how many core concepts of startups and product building you've either invented or popularized. So what I know, obviously Lean methodology, then there's the term MVP, then there's the term pivot, and then also I think A/B testing, customer development, continuous deployment, vanity metrics as a term, I'm guessing there's many more, and then the Long-Term Stock Exchange. And I think the theme I get from this is there's a lot of first principles thinking that you've done, and so just a couple of questions here. One is, did you think you'd have this much impact on startup culture and language? And then just, where do you think this comes from, this first principles thinking that you seem to be really good at?
turns.zh: 太棒了，接下来我们要深入探讨这些话题。首先我想说的是，人们对您在创业和产品构建领域发明或推广的核心概念重视不足。比如精益方法论、最小可行产品（MVP）、业务转型（pivot）、A/B测试、客户开发、持续部署，还有“虚荣度指标”这样的术语。当然还有长期证券交易所。我觉得您始终秉持许多第一性原理的思考方式。接下来有几个问题：您是否预料到自己会对创业文化和行业用语产生如此深远的影响？您认为这种善于运用第一性原理的能力源自何处？

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Well, first of all, thank you for saying all that. That's giving me too much credit, but I like the idea that it's going to balance out the too little credit I ostensibly get somewhere else, that's great. To answer your question, no, I didn't know this was going to happen. This is so embarrassing to admit now, but just to give you a sense of how different the world is now than at the time of the financial crisis, I was so embarrassed to be blogging, that I didn't put my name on the blog. I published it anonymously because it wasn't a thing that people did and people told me it would be career suicide. And there were so few startup bloggers at that time, that the top three all reached out to me personally because they saw it in their referrer logs on their website. That's how little traffic they got, that when a new person started writing about their thing and linking to them, they were like, "Who is this guy? What's going on?" It was a very different time. (00:08:07): And I had just finished a startup. I had left a startup that was being successful, and I had this reputation among VCs that I could make engineering teams be supernaturally productive. I had the magic pixie dust. And so, they would ask me to come in and work with their teams and I would be like, "No, listen, honestly, I'm not that special. It's nothing to do with me. It's just this framework. I have these ideas that are helpful on a team when they adopt them." And they would pat me on the head and be like, "Yeah, kid, I'm sure that's great, but can you please bring the magic pixie dust to my company anyway?" (00:08:38): And I would go and have these meetings, and I'm not making this up, people would yell at me in the meeting. I would get yelled at. In fact, I would be asked not very kindly to leave, and I'd be like, "I don't understand. What are you yelling... Why are you mad at me? You asked me for this meeting." And they'd be like... I'm just telling you what I witnessed with my own eyes. We at IMVU, we shipped product 50 times a day on average at a time when people were lucky to be doing it monthly if they were really advanced. Remember, it wasn't that long ago that we put the year the product came out in the name of the product. That tells you what cycle times used to be. That was considered normal, and people were like, "That's impossible. That could never work." (00:09:15): And at that time, I wasn't even propounding a theory or anything, I was just explaining what I had seen and people couldn't believe it. And so I had this great idea, if I write some of these stories down, then when someone asked me for these... I was doing these meetings all the time. I didn't understand the way Silicon Valley worked at that time, I didn't understand why this was happening to me, having these meetings, and I said, "I'll write the story down and then I'll send people the essay, and if they think it's crazy, then we don't have to have the meeting and I won't get yelled at." That was really as far ahead as I was thinking at that time. And then it basically took over my life, and I was being asked to speak, but people really wanted to unmask the anonymity. Who is this person? And so I came clean, I identified myself and started writing and speaking and working with companies, and it became a whirlwind. (00:09:58): The first principles part of it, I don't know, I've always been wired that way. I feel like maybe I'm a failed scientist. I wish I was actually good at chemistry or something. I could have actually been a real scientist, but I always really had a respect for the truth for scientific thinking. That was a big cultural value that I was raised with. My parents are doctors, it was just definitely part of my upbringing, and I was really into reading stuff that worked that way. So, it was very natural for me. I felt like as I had success as an entrepreneur, I wanted to know, why does this work? And people gave me advice. All the advice used to be of the form, "Steve Jobs once did this thing, so if you do it too, you'll be like Steve Jobs." And it's like, well, he also wore the black turtleneck. Is that also part of the... Help me understand, why does it work and is it still appropriate? Does it make sense for that industry or not? I didn't like these just so stories. (00:10:44): And I realized looking back, I didn't have this understanding at the time, but looking back, I feel like first principles thinking, it really has two components that people pretend are one thing, and it's more one than the other. A lot of my work is just descriptive. It's not actually telling people what to do, it's simply giving a name and a concept to a thing that already happens. That's the funniest part. In the early wave of criticism against Lean Startup, people were very angry at the idea that I was saying that a startup is an experiment like, "You can't treat a startup like an experiment." I was like, "Well, you could treat it however you want, but it is an experiment." People would like, "Well, people don't like the concept of pivot." This anti-pivot people, anti-MVP people every once in a while come out of the woodwork still to complain about it. (00:11:25): It's like, "well, I'm not telling you that you should pivot. I'm just saying that is what it's called when you change the strategy, but try to have fidelity to the vision." It needs a name because we do it all the time and even when we don't do it, we talk about doing it. We can't reason about it, we can't... And so this is descriptive part, and then that's the real work, honestly, is just saying what is... To me, the big question from the beginning was, what is a startup really? Why is it so different from a big company? Why are none of the best practices that I learned in my career work? It was like a survival mechanism, I want to know. And then once you've identified what it is and laid out the original principles of what you're trying to do, the prescriptive parts are just a matter of deductive logic. (00:12:10): It's like, "Well, given that we've made this hypothesis, what are the implications of that?" And of course, the prescriptive parts are important because that's how you learn whether your hypothesis is correct. So, that's the other thing I think people don't appreciate. People call me a first principles thinker, which I love that, it's a big compliment, but I feel like it conjures up for people this idea that I sit in a cave for years and years and conjure up the magic idea. It's like, no, I wish people had all the outtakes of all the concepts I've tried. Lean Startup was not my first try, the conceptual vocabulary. It's not the first time I got it right. It came through a lot of trial and error, a lot of trying to figure out what works and doesn't work, first in my own career, in my own work, then trying to give advice to other people and trying to translate what worked for me to see what would work for them, and then to answer the questions that I thought were the natural ones. (00:12:57): Under what circumstances does it work and when would it not be appropriate? What predictions does the theory make that we could then go see if are true or not true? And then the bigger picture thing is, what are we really doing here? What does success even look like? That, I think, is the thing we all really grapple with is it's very easy to come up with a theory or a method or a process that produces the maximum of something, but then it's like, "Is that thing good? Is that actually helping us accomplish some kind of goal?" And so, I think that first principles thinking is very helpful for that too, but I don't know. I guess to really answer your question, the true answer is I don't know. I've just always felt like I was wired that way. I have a love of ideas and want to know why things work.
turns.zh:
好的，首先，感谢你说了这么多。这让我觉得自己被过度赞誉了，但我喜欢这种平衡我明显被其他地方低估的观点，这很棒。回答你的问题，不，我当时并不知道会发生这种事。现在回想起来真是难为情，但正好能让你感受到金融危机时期和现在世界的巨大差异——当时我对写博客感到非常不好意思，所以没有署名。我匿名发布了文章，因为那时没人这么做，别人还警告我这会毁掉职业生涯。当时创业博主极少，排名前三的博主主动联系我，因为他们在网站引荐日志里发现了我的内容。可见当时流量有多低，以至于当有人开始写关于他们的内容并链接到他们时，他们会惊讶地问：“这人是谁？怎么回事？” 那真是完全不同的时代了。（00:08:07）那时我刚结束一家创业公司。我离开了一家成功的创业公司，在风投界树立了能让工程团队超高效率的名声，被称为拥有“魔法仙尘”。他们邀请我去指导他们的团队时，我会说：“不，听着，说真的，我没那么特别。这只是个框架。我有一些理念，只要团队采纳就能提升效率。”他们就会拍拍我的头，说：“行吧，小子，听起来很棒，但能不能把你的魔法仙尘带到我的公司来？”（00:08:38）我去参加那些会议，毫不夸张地说，人们会对我大吼大叫。我被要求离开时还会反问：“我不明白，你们为什么对我发火？明明是你们约我来开会的啊。”他们只能回答……我只是在讲述亲眼所见的事。我们IMVU当时平均每天发布50次产品更新，而当时其他公司如果进展顺利，每月发布一次产品就很幸运了。记得不久前我们还在产品名称里写上发布年份。这足以说明当时的开发周期有多长。这被视为常态，人们会说：“这不可能，永远行不通。”（00:09:15）那时我甚至没有提出什么理论，只是描述亲身经历，可人们就是难以置信。于是我有了个好主意，把这些故事写下来。每次开会时，我都会遇到不理解硅谷运作方式的人，他们不明白为什么要开会，就说：“我会读你的文章，如果觉得疯狂就不用开会了。”这就是我当时的全部思考。后来这件事占据了我的生活，人们要求我演讲，但都想揭开我的匿名身份。于是我公开了身份，开始写作、演讲和与公司合作，一切都变得忙碌起来。
科学思维。这是我从小被灌输的一个重要文化价值观。我的父母都是医生，所以这种思维方式深深融入了我的成长过程中。我特别喜欢阅读那些遵循这种思维模式的书籍和文章，所以这对我来说非常自然。当我作为创业者取得成功后，我总想探究其中的奥秘。人们给我的建议通常是：“史蒂夫·乔布斯曾这样做过，所以你效仿他就能成为乔布斯。”但我会反问：“他还穿黑色高领衫呢，这也是创新的一部分吗？”我需要人们帮助我理解：为什么这种方法有效？它是否仍然适用？它对特定行业是否有意义？我不喜欢那些空洞的成功故事。

（00:10:44）回顾过去，我当时并不明白这些道理，但现在看来，我所谓的“第一性原理思维”其实包含两个部分——人们常把它们混为一谈，但其实一个更重要。我的大部分工作都是描述性的。我并非在教人如何做事，而是在为已然存在的现象命名和赋予概念。这才是最有趣的地方。在“精益创业”理念初期遭遇批评时，人们对“创业是实验”的观点极为不满，声称“不能把创业当作实验”。我回应道：“你当然可以随心所欲地看待它，但它确实就是实验。”还有人反对“转型”和“最小可行产品”理念——这些反对者时不时跳出来抱怨。（00:11:25）我解释道：“我不是说要你转型，而是说当你改变策略时，这叫‘转型’，但要忠实于愿景。”这种命名方式很有必要，因为我们一直在这么做，即便不这么做，也会谈论这些概念。我们无法用理性分析它，只能直观理解。这是描述性部分，而真正的工作在于推理逻辑。

（00:12:10）比如，“基于这个假设，会有哪些影响？”当然，推理部分很重要，因为它能验证假设是否正确。这也是我认为人们不易理解的另一层含义。人们称我为“第一性原理思考者”，我很感激这称赞，但总觉得这让人误以为我深居简出、异想天开。其实不然，我希望人们能看到我尝试过的所有概念的成果。精益创业并非我的首次尝试，也不是我首次掌握概念词汇。这也不是我首次成功。它源于大量试错，从自身职业生涯到为他人提供建议，努力总结适合自己的方法，再解答那些看似显而易见的问题：在何种情况下它有效？何时不适用？该理论作出了哪些预测？我们又该如何验证这些预测？
然后更宏观的层面来讲，我们在这里到底在做什么？成功到底应该是什么样子的？我觉得这才是我们所有人真正需要深思的问题。制定一个能产出最优结果的理论、方法或流程很容易，但随后就会产生疑问：“这样做真的好吗？它真的能帮助我们达成某个目标吗？”因此，我认为第一性原理思维对此也非常有帮助，但说实话，我也不确定。或许要真正回答你的问题，最真实的答案就是我不知道。我只是天生就对各种想法充满热情，总想探究事物背后的原理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to me, a couple of takeaways from what you just shared. One is just you're wired to think in this specific way of thinking very logically, scientifically, I have a similar feeling where someone tells me a story... The way I started writing partly is people kept asking me questions about how Airbnb did stuff because they're building their marketplace. I'm like, "Here's what they did, but who knows if that was the way to have done it?"
turns.zh: 对我而言，从你刚才分享的内容中得出几个关键点：首先，你天生就倾向于以这种极其逻辑化、科学化的思维方式思考。这种感觉我也很熟悉——比如有人给我讲故事时……我开始写作的部分原因是，有人老是问我Airbnb是如何做事的，因为他们正在搭建自己的市场平台。我就想：“他们是这么做的，但谁知道这是否是最优解呢？”

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Exactly. Did they succeed because of that or in spite of that?
turns.zh: 没错。他们是因为这样做才成功，还是不顾这种方式反而成功了？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's dig into the Lean Startup method and methodology. It feels like we haven't heard an update on just how things are going, where it's going, how popular it continues to be. I'm curious just, what's your sense of the state of the Lean methodology in the Lean Startup movement?
turns.zh: 让我们深入探讨一下精益创业的方法和理念。感觉我们很久没听到关于它进展如何、未来走向如何、持续受欢迎程度如何的最新消息了。我很好奇，在精益创业运动中，精益方法论的现状如何？

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Oh, it's an interesting question. We used to do a Lean Startup conference every year, and then I stopped because of COVID and we haven't resumed yet. So, it was like we used to have an annual opportunity to bring people together, assess the state of things, hear the latest updates and stories, and then I really feel the lack of it, I miss it. We tried to do online versions, but it didn't feel right to me. And that's partly COVID and the thing that our world has been going through the last few years, but it's also partly I didn't understand what it would be like to start a movement until I'd actually done it. And I remember the first conferences we did, the first events we did had the feeling of a religious revival. People were like, "We've got the new thing. We are going to stick it to the man." (00:15:04): And I really thought, "My job is going to be to lead these hordes into battle." I really had a martial metaphor. I used it just a second ago, combat of ideas. I was ready for, the old ideas are going to fight us to the death and we're going to win it, and it's not like that at all. We charge onto the field and no other army ever came to charge us back, just we won by default because the people who were doing it the old way didn't really like it or want... It was very few defenders of the old way. There were very few people who came out and said, "Actually, no, Stage-Gate is actually still the correct product idea. You've got it wrong." It never happened, and in fact, the fancy startup people went from dismissing it as totally pointless to complaining that it was overhyped and over before ever passing through the intervening stage of finding out what it was. That was really interesting. I'll never forget, TechCrunch had an article, this is years and years ago about how Lean Startup is overhyped, and I was like, "You haven't even talked..." That was the first entry point to talking about it. I was like, "Could you at least learn to use the word pivot correctly and then criticize it for being overhyped? Is that all possible?" So, it went from insurgent revival to just the default thing that people did. Even the people that disagree have to carry the meme in order to criticize it. So, it was fascinating to find myself on the other side of this thing, and I would meet young founders coming into the industry for the first time, and they're like, "It seems obvious," and I'm like, "It was only five years ago that people thought this was so crazy they're yelling at me, now you think it's obvious?" (00:16:48): It's really interesting to have something go from controversial to obvious, and of course, tons of people who were really opposed to it at the beginning came back. Now they say that they knew it all along and they were my big... You see how it changes people's minds. So, it's hard to generate that religious energy and excitement around something that everyone views as obvious, and it really was hard for my... Just as an ego matter, I want the validation of the winning and the this, and I realized at a certain point that the victory is not that this fancy company used it or whatever, the victory actually is in the stories that people tell me about how the book was helpful to them. (00:17:26): That's the whole ball game. No one had to lose in order for us to win. People don't do this as much anymore, but occasionally someone still who wants to make a fight between Lean Startup and Agile or Agile and design thinking or this and that... And I tried really hard. If you look at Lean Startup, it's full of citations and connections to Six Sigma and lean manufacturing and design thinking and customer development and DevOps and software craftsmanship and everything I could find. I really wanted to show how these things work together, and then we went through a phase where people wanted me to make it into a religion for real. People used to write me and say, "So-and-so on the internet is right about Lean Startup in they're wrong. You need to make them stop." It's like, "What power do you think I have to make someone stop writing? I think they can write whatever they want." (00:18:13): And then the other thing that people said was, "Well, Lean Startup is about this particular set of practices. If someone finds a new practice, they're at heretic and need to be excommunicated." And it's like, "Guys, no, no, no. I wrote extensively in the book... Did you read? It's a scientific theory, which means that whatever works is Lean Startup. So if someone comes up with something new and it works, we can't be threatened and upset about it, we have to adopt it." Well, when you have that attitude that whatever works is the thing that the truth is what matters and people's quiet moments of helpfulness, that's our metric of success, it kind of takes the hype and drama and stuff that drives press coverage and what takes it all out of it, and I don't miss it at all. I feel much happier doing that than I ever did when... I used to travel a lot and do a lot more public stuff, and I think partly, again, one of the changes of COVID and conferences went away for a while, so it was a quiet time, but I feel like it's actually been really amazing. That's what victory looks like. They don't throw you a parade and say the thing... And even though people who are your critics will still grumble about it, but at the end of the day, the new entrepreneurs who come in just take for granted that this is the conceptual vocabulary of entrepreneurship, and then they do with it what they will, and I've learned to really appreciate that. As much as my ego, of course, likes to get into fights with people. It's like, "No, that's actually better, and that's what winning looks like."
turns.zh:
哦，这真是个有趣的问题。我们过去每年都会举办“精益创业大会”，但因为新冠疫情暂停至今尚未恢复。过去，那次年度盛会为我们提供了汇聚行业精英、评估行业现状、聆听最新动态与成功案例的宝贵机会。如今我深深怀念它，尽管尝试过线上版本，但始终感觉不够味儿。这既源于疫情影响，也源于我直到亲身实践才真正理解如何发起一场运动。记得最初的会议和活动充满宗教复兴般的激情，人们高呼“我们找到了新思路，要与旧势力抗争到底”。当时我满脑子都是“我的职责就是带领这支队伍冲锋陷阵”，甚至用了军事比喻——“思想之战”。我以为旧有观念会拼命抵抗，而我们必将取胜。但现实远非如此。我们冲锋上阵，却无对手反击，因为旧有模式的拥护者寥寥无几。鲜少有人站出来说：“其实 Stage-Gate 才是正确的产品开发路径，你们理解错了。” 这种情况从未发生过。相反，那些曾经对精益创业嗤之以鼻的人，一转身就抱怨它被过度炒作、名不副实，甚至在未深入了解其本质之前就匆忙下结论。这真是耐人寻味。多年前《TechCrunch》就发表文章称精益创业被过度宣传，我当时反驳道：“你们甚至没谈过……” 这成了我参与讨论的切入点。我质问：“你们能不能先正确理解‘pivot’这个词，再来批判它被过度炒作？” 精益创业从叛逆运动逐渐成为行业标配，即便持反对意见的人也不得不借用这个概念来批判它。亲身经历这个转变过程真是令人惊讶。我遇到初入行的年轻创业者，他们说：“这似乎显而易见。” 而我回想五年前人们还对此嗤之以鼻，现在却视为理所当然？从争议到共识的过程实在耐人寻味。当然，许多最初反对者后来也回心转意。现在他们声称自己一直深知其价值，称赞我是他们的启蒙者。这可见人们观念转变之迅速。然而，要在所有人都视为理所当然的事物上激发宗教般的热情与兴奋，实在不易。就个人而言，我渴望胜利的认可，渴望证明自己的价值。但某个时刻我意识到，真正的胜利不在于某家大公司采用了精益创业，而在于人们讲述书籍如何帮助他们的故事。（00:17:26）这才是关键所在。我们的胜利无需他人的失败来衬托。如今人们不再频繁将精益创业与敏捷、敏捷与设计思维、各种方法论割裂比较……我曾竭力捍卫精益创业的完整性。但回看精益创业的发展历程，处处可见与六西格玛、瀑布模型等的交叉引用，这让我不得不反思：我们是否真的需要用对错二分法来定义胜利？
西格玛管理、精益生产、设计思维、客户开发、DevOps、软件工艺，以及我能找到的所有相关概念。我真的很想展示这些理念如何协同运作。但后来我们经历了一个阶段，人们希望我把这套理论奉为神圣教条。过去常有人写信给我，说：“网上某某对精益创业的理解是错误的，你必须让他们停止这种错误言论。”我只能回应：“你以为我有权力让别人闭嘴吗？他们想写什么就写什么好了。” （00:18:13）还有人说：“精益创业只讲一套特定的实践方法。如果有人发现新方法，他们就是异端，应该被驱逐出教。” 我又说：“各位，别这样。我在书里已经充分论证了……你们读过书吗？精益创业是一套科学理论，任何有效的做法都属于精益创业。所以如果有人提出新方法且行之有效，我们不必为此感到威胁或不安，应该欣然接纳。” 当你秉持“只要有效就是真理”的态度，并感恩于人们默默提供的帮助时，这才是衡量成功的标准。它消解了媒体炒作和戏剧性冲突，带走了一切浮华与闹剧。我对此心怀感激，远胜于过去……我过去常四处奔波，参加各种公开活动。但新冠疫情让会议暂停，人们暂时冷静下来，这段时间反而让我倍感充实。胜利的模样就是这样。没有人为你举办庆功仪式，也没有人表扬你……即便批评者仍会抱怨，但最终新晋创业者们会自然而然地将这些理念视为创业的核心词汇，然后灵活运用。对此我深有体会。当然，我的自尊心有时还是想与人争执。但我最终意识到：“不，这才是真正的胜利。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting that it's just you've done so well in communicating these ideas that it's just become part of the culture, and people don't even think about, "Oh, Eric Ries came up with all these things." I also feel like people push back at you on the things they disagree with, and then they never give you credit for the things that work great. It's only like, "Oh, no, MVPs don't work anymore."
turns.zh: 真有趣的是，正是因为你把这些理念传达得如此出色，它们才成为文化的一部分，人们甚至不会去想：“哦，这些都是埃里克·里斯提出的啊。”我还发现，当人们对某些观点持不同意见时，他们会反驳你，但当某些方法确实有效时，却从不给你应有的赞誉。比如，他们会说：“哦，不，MVP已经不行了。”

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Once a year at least, someone still writes to me and says that we should have used a different term for MVP, that the misconceptions around MVP are driven by the choice of the term. And I always write them back and say like, "Please tell me the better term and popularize it and I'll use it. It's a great idea." I'm more aware of the limitations than anybody else. And I'll tell you another thing that I think people don't appreciate enough, everyone wants to be a thought leader these days. It's like a disease. When Clay Christensen died, I knew him and admired him a great deal, and his endorsement of my work was one of the most important... (00:20:39): For me, from the old guard of management thinkers, for him to say that it was worthwhile was really a big deal to me. And yet there was this big debate, it's now a little bit older now, about whether he's responsible for all the bad things people have done in the name of disruption. And the first part of me is like, "That's an outrageous slander on Clay. That's so unfair, a bunch of tech bros like use disruption as a code word for all kinds of dumb stuff has nothing to do with his theory, has nothing to do with his work." It's like, "Have they even read the work, man?" I was one of his defenders, and especially after he passed, I was very emotional about it, it's not fair. (00:21:16): But then the more that I've sat with it, the more I thought, "Gosh, maybe we are a little bit responsible for the things we put into the world," and it's terrifying because of course, you can't control what people do, you can't control... A lot of people are willfully ignorant. Whenever someone says something where I'm like, "Gosh, five seconds on Wikipedia, and they could have found out the truth about the thing they're talking about." So, we live in an era where ignorance is optional, that's cool, but also a little bit scary. So I think taking on that responsibility, this is true for anyone who makes a product. I think it's not actually unique to authors at all. When you make something, put it out into the world, on the one hand, you don't have any control about what happens next, and yet I do think we bear a certain responsibility about, was it in fact a net positive? Was it helpful to people? (00:21:59): It's part of what motivates me to try to really get it right and not just get it right for my own satisfaction, but get it right as evidenced by what happens when people use it. And that's why testing and experimentation is such a big part of my life and my theory. To me, that's how we square the circle of our responsibility in a highly uncertain world is you go find out what happened when people use the idea and if it's not right, even after their misunderstandings, it's still not right, then you've got to make it better and find a way to communicate it more clearly, so it's kind of an eternal challenge, but I think an important one.
turns.zh: 每年至少都会有人写信给我，建议我们应该用别的术语来替代MVP，认为MVP的误解源于术语选择。我每次都会回复他们说：“请告诉我更好的术语并推广它，我会用的。这是个好主意。”我比任何人都清楚其局限性。我还要说一句，我觉得人们对此重视不够——如今每个人都想成为思想领袖，这简直像一种病态。克莱·克里斯滕森去世时，我认识他并非常敬重他。他对我的工作的认可对我意义非凡……（00:20:39）：对我来说，作为管理思想界的老将，他说这值得推广，这对我意义重大。然而围绕他是否要为打着颠覆旗号做出的种种恶行负责，曾有一场激烈争论。起初我会想：“这简直是对克莱的恶意攻击，太不公平了。那些自诩精通技术的家伙把‘颠覆’当作各种愚蠢行为的代名词，这和他的理论毫无关系，和他的工作也毫无关联。”我会说：“他们到底有没有读过他的著作啊？”我是他的捍卫者之一，尤其是在他去世后，我情绪激动得难以自持，这太不公平了。（00:21:16）：但随着时间推移，我越发意识到：“天啊，也许我们对自己创造的东西负有一定责任。” 这很可怕，因为你无法控制人们的所作所为，很多人故意无知。每当有人说些让我无语的话时，我总会想：“只要花五秒钟在维基百科上查查，他们就能明白真相。” 我们生活在一个无知可选的时代，这很棒，但也令人担忧。所以我认为承担这种责任——这适用于任何产品创造者。我认为这并非作者独有。当你创造出某样东西并推向世界时，一方面你无法控制后续的发展，但我确实认为我们对其是否真正带来积极影响负有责任。这对人们是否有帮助？（00:21:59）：这就是激励我努力把事情做好的原因——不只是为了满足自己的虚荣心，而是通过人们实际使用后的反馈来验证是否成功。这就是为什么测试和实验成为我生活和理论的重要组成部分。对我来说，在高度不确定的世界中履行责任的关键在于：去观察人们使用这个理念后的结果。即便在他们误解之后，如果它仍然不正确，那就必须改进并找到更清晰的沟通方式。这是个永恒的挑战，但我认为这很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those same lines, is there a misconception of Lean Startup or any of the other things you put out that just really frustrates you, that just is a recurring misconception that people just continue to get wrong?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，有没有关于精益创业或你提到的其他概念的误解，让你特别抓狂，或者说那些反复出现、人们始终理解错误的误解？

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: I wrote an article, God, five or 10 years ago. God, I can't even remember how many years ago now. It was like Top Misconceptions About Lean Startup, and it was like, "Number one, lean means cheap, so if you're doing Lean Startup, it means you're not raising money." And it's like, "That's not true." And then kind of I remember what they are... And they're all still prevalent, nothing's changed. I could write that same article today. It's like, "Lean is opposed to having a vision. If you were really visionary, you wouldn't do experimentation. Experimentation leads to local maxima," and whatever. (00:23:20): I read it in somebody's book that that's what Lean is about. And I was like, "Man, did I forget to write it in the..." I was so gaslighted that I actually went back and cracked open a copy of the Lean Startup, and I was like, "On what page do I address this?" It was like on page nine in the introduction, one of the first things in the book, I was like, "Phew, I did say it," so that's pretty common, that turn the crank thing about optimization, that's pretty common, and then pivots, people perennially misunderstand what a pivot is, and again, whether that's a descriptive or a prescriptive thing is really tricky. (00:23:54): I feel like at this point people are just being willfully ignorant. It's okay to criticize Lean Startup, that's no problem. It doesn't bother me. I think it's good to do, it's healthy to do so, but to just trot out those same old things, how does that advance the state-of-the-art? And how does that help entrepreneurs in any way? And I'm not even really sure what they're trying to accomplish by doing that. That's the thing that I've grown confused about is, what is the purpose of this discourse, other than just to kind be reflexively contrarian? I don't know.
turns.zh: 五年或十年前，我写过一篇文章。天啊，我甚至记不清是几年前了。那篇文章叫《关于精益创业的十大误区》，当时有人说：“第一，精益意味着低成本，所以如果你在做精益创业，就意味着你不融资。”我当时就说：“这根本不对。”然后我又回想了一下那些误区……它们至今依然普遍存在，毫无改观。我今天还能写同样的文章。比如“精益与愿景相悖。如果你真的有远见，就不会做实验。实验会导致局部最优解”之类的。（00:23:20）我曾在某本书里读到有人这么解释精益创业。我当时就想：“天啊，我是不是忘了在书里写这部分了……” 我被误导得太厉害了，以至于我翻出《精益创业》一书，查找相关内容。结果发现，就在引言部分的第九页，书里最先提到的内容之一。我松了一口气：“呼，我确实提到过这个。” 关于优化的“不断尝试”这种说法很常见，关于转型的误解也屡见不鲜。判断这是描述性还是规范性的东西真的很棘手。（00:23:54）我觉得现在人们就是故意无知。批评精益创业没问题，我不介意。我认为这很好，很健康，但老是翻出那些老掉牙的观点，这对推动行业进步有何帮助？对创业者又有何益处？我甚至不确定他们这么做有什么目的。最让我困惑的是，这种讨论的意义何在？除了故作反叛之外还有什么别的意义吗？我真的不明白。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And get some likes on Twitter/X.
turns.zh: 或许你说得对。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Maybe you're right.
turns.zh: 也许你说得对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along those same lines, so you wrote the book 12 years ago. If you could go back and change something in the book, is there something that you would want to change?
turns.zh: 那么顺着这个思路，你12年前写了那本书。如果让你回到过去修改书中内容，有什么想改的地方吗？

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Oh man, I would change everything about it. It's actually why I won't let myself do it. When I was a consumer of books, I hated it when authors would come out with a second edition that would destroy what was beautiful about the first edition, including the mistakes because in their attempt to put disclaimers on everything and make everything more nuanced, you'd totally lose the thrust of the argument of the thing they were trying to do, and their own becoming famous really messes with you psychologically. So, you don't want to expose your readers to that. Go get therapy, don't destroy the thing that made your book amazing. So as an author, of course, I think so many elements of it could be improved. The one that is the most glaring to me... Well, I guess there's two. I'll mention two just because they're relevant. (00:25:26): One is I'm a little embarrassed, there's a chapter towards the end of the book where I talk about the scaling of Lean Startup. So it's like, "Okay, you've had success. Now, what are the principles for how you scale up a big enterprise now that has many Lean Startups within it?" And stuff like that, and I don't think I wrote anything wrong in that section, but I really cringe to read it now because it's so blithe and just like, "Step one, do this. Step two, do that." It makes it sound so easy and so simple. (00:25:53): And of course, I've subsequently written a whole book longer than Lean Startup just to illuminate those principles and explain how they work in real life because I actually had the privilege of getting to go do that with companies at really extraordinary scale. So, I'm a little embarrassed now to be like, "I made it sound so easy." I hate to mislead any entrepreneurs into thinking any part of entrepreneurship is going to be easy because it's just setting people up for disappointment. And the other funny bit is, you know that meme on Reddit, the Star Wars meme where Anakin Skywalker says, "I'm going to change the world for the better," and then pause, and then she's like, "For the better, right?" I feel like that is the meme of our time for the tech industry. Every company was about changing the world and we forgot to ask, for the better? I always just took it for granted that our goal was to make the world a better place. That's the values I was raised with. That's what I thought we were doing, and I was railing about it for a while. I would get depressed. Remember, don't be evil? And there's been all these moments in the tech industry where it seemed like we were going to really do something extraordinary, and then just the things that these companies become is so depressing. And I was like, " Well, I at least made it clear." And then I was like, "Did I?" (00:27:04): Again, I actually went back and reopened the book and I was like, "Did I tell anybody that they should change the world?" And if I did, I assume I specified for the better, and it's actually right there in black and white. Right in the introduction of Lean Startup, one of the... It's like a throwaway line, "This is the technique that will give the entrepreneurs of tomorrow the tools they need to change the world." And I'm like, "No, I should have said for the better. I didn't know I had to say it. I thought it was obvious. I thought we all agreed." So, I kind of feel like that is also a major oversight and I'm making light of it now, but it's had catastrophic consequences. Not really, I don't think Lean Startup has led people in that way. I think it has much more to do with other social forces, but I feel bad that I missed my chance to take a stand on something that has turned out to be quite important.
turns.zh:
天哪，我真想把这本书改得面目全非。这就是为什么我根本不愿意去改它。当我还是个读者的时候，我特别讨厌有些作者出第二版，把第一版的精华全毁掉——包括那些错误。作者们总想在每个细节上加注释，让一切都更微妙，结果却完全偏离了原意的核心论点。而他们自己出名之后的心态变化，更是让人心理上难以接受。所以你不能让读者遭受这种折磨。去找心理治疗吧，不要毁掉让你的书如此出色的东西。  

作为作者，我当然觉得这本书有很多可以改进的地方。最让我无语的是……嗯，应该有两个方面吧。我就说两个吧，因为它们很相关。（00:25:26）：一个是有点尴尬，书里快结尾的时候有一章讲精益创业的扩展。当时我写的是：“好，你成功了。现在，如何在一个内部包含多个精益创业项目的大型企业中推广这些原则？”之类的。我觉得自己那部分写得没错，但现在再看简直幼稚得离谱。“第一步，干这个。第二步，干那个。”说得轻而易举，简单得很。（00:25:53）：当然，后来我又写了一本比《精益创业》长得多的书，就是为了阐释那些原则，说明它们在现实中的应用。因为我有幸能在真正大规模的公司里实践这些理念。所以现在回想起来，我有点不好意思说：“我把它写得太简单了。” 我不想误导任何创业者，让他们以为创业任何部分都会轻松，因为这只会让人失望。另一个搞笑的梗是，你知道Reddit上的那个《星球大战》梗吗，阿纳金·天行者说：“我要让世界变得更美好。”然后停顿一下，然后她说：“变得更美好，对吧？” 我觉得这就是我们这个时代科技行业的梗。每个公司都说要改变世界，却忘了问“变得更好吗？”我一直理所当然地认为我们的目标就是让世界更美好。这些价值观伴随我成长，我以为我们就是在做这件事，还为此抱怨了一阵，变得抑郁。记得那句“别作恶”吗？科技行业曾有过很多看似要做出非凡改变的时刻，结果这些公司最后变成的样子实在令人失望。我当时就想：“好吧，我至少把道理讲清楚了。” 然后又自问：“我真的讲清楚了吗？” （00:27:04）：再说，我重新翻开书，发现自己写过：“我告诉过任何人要改变世界吗？” 如果写过，我想应该明确是“变得更好”，而这句话就写在书里——在《精益创业》的引言里，有一句随口一提的话：“这项技术将为未来的创业者提供改变世界所需的工具。” 我当时想：“不，我应该说‘变得更好’。我以为这很明显。我以为大家都认同。” 所以我觉得这也是个重大疏忽，现在拿来开玩笑，但它带来了灾难性的后果。其实我不认为《精益创业》误导了人们。我觉得更多是其他社会力量在起作用，但我为自己错过机会而感到遗憾。
就某件后来被证明极为重要的事情表明立场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you saw me tweet a call for people to ask questions.
turns.zh: 嗯，你看到我发推特呼吁大家提问了。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Yes, I'm really excited.
turns.zh: 是的，我真的很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I have a few questions from the audience. The first is around the concept of MVPs. So Karri Saarinen, who was actually on the podcast recently-
turns.zh: 现在我有几个观众提的问题。第一个是关于MVP的概念。卡里·萨里宁（Karri Saarinen）最近参加了我们的播客——

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Oh, great.
turns.zh: 哦，太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... Founder of Linear, had a question around MVPs. And his question is essentially, If you still believe that MVPs, essentially shipping very basic versions and iterating is the way to go, given that user expectations have risen a lot in any markets, iOS apps, for example, web productivity software, things like that.
turns.zh: ……Linear公司的创始人，他对MVP提出了一个问题。他的问题核心是，鉴于用户对iOS应用、网页生产力软件等产品的期望值大幅提高，如果你仍然认为MVP（即先推出非常基础的版本然后不断迭代）是正确的策略，那你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: I love that question because first of all, I get it a lot, and also it's important for us to really understand. People think that MVP is about a specific tactic. So, an MVP is like a bare bones, stripped down the thing that will crash your computer, but it's not anything to do with MVP. MVP is simply for whatever the hypothesis is that we're trying to test, what is the most efficient way to get the validation we need about whether a hypothesis is true or not? And so, part of a successful test is to understand what are the demands of customers in our market. Now, the funny part is people have a real fear of failure in product we all have this deep, deep, deep fear. So the first answer is, you think user expectations are high in the iOS App Store, you should try the purchasers of battery backup systems for data centers or people who build deep sea oil drilling machines or jet engine. (00:29:22): I've worked with companies where the standards are actually really high and it makes iOS apps seem like pretty basic. It's like, "Well, nothing blows up like your app," but even in these really high end industries in really high stake situations, the cost of offering someone to buy something that they don't like, it's really not that high. They just say no, and a lot of MVP is just about containing the liability of making a mistake. So yes, one of the things I really encourage people to do is go find 10 customers, not 10 million, but find 10 customers. Get them to use the product and have them tell you what's awful. That's okay, and I used to be so upset... When I used to launch a product if customers would argue with me, people used to be like, "You idiot, I can't believe you launched this product without features X, Y, Z. They're so essential." (00:30:11): And I would be like, "You're wrong..." I'd got to get mad at them, but then I got a little smarter. I'd be like, "X, Y, Z, you say?" And I'd be like taking notes, "Oh, interesting." Now, sometimes X, Y, Z would be the exact next three features of my roadmap, and again, I would want to argue with them as, "I know knew that..." And I eventually used to be like, "Oh, thank you for that wise feedback." And then when we launched X, Y, Z, they would feel a sense of ownership. "Wow, I'm the one who told him to do that. He wouldn't have even done it." But of course, the thing we're really afraid of as entrepreneurs, I think if we're really honest, it's not that people say, "You idiot, you didn't launch without X, Y, Z," people will say, "You idiot, you launched without A, B, C." (00:30:44): And you're like, "What the hell is A, B, C?" Never heard of that. That's the much more common response that I get. So, let's grant the premise of the question that expectations are high, and if we launch an app and it doesn't meet people's expectations, they won't like it. First of all, what really are the consequences of that? In an early part of Lean Startup, we had to do a lot to explain to people the difference between a product launch and a marketing launch. And you can launch the product to customers without telling anybody that you did that. It's okay. No one's going to find out, it's not going to be big news. And of course, once you're a big successful company, that's a totally different issue where now you put your corporate brand on stuff, but if you're an actual startup, nobody cares. So, it's okay to try it. (00:31:29): But the other thing that I think people don't appreciate is that MVP is very flexible. So, if you tell me... When I work with entrepreneurs, I'm like, "Listen, I'm sorry, our customer is... The bar is here and the thing just has to be that good." I'm like, "Excellent, and it can't have very many features, I guess, can it?" They're like, "Well, what do you mean?" "So, you just told me the bar is way up there, so we better do just the one critical feature at that level of quality, and then if that works, we'll do the next one." And then of course they're like, "Oh, no, no, no, I need to do all the features at all the quality." It's like, "Well, then what are we testing?" It's like, "By the time you find out whether that's any good..." And if you look at the pivot stories, I'm sure you found this too. (00:32:06): Very often 90% of the work in the first version is thrown away no matter how high quality it was. In fact, as an engineer, that was part of my original disillusionment with the Agile software movement then ultimately with Lean Startup is that people promised me that if I followed these best practices, I would eliminate waste from my work, but if I build something that customers don't want, that's the ultimate waste and nobody protected me from that. So, I don't really care how high quality the initial MVP is because quality is defined by the customer. And if we don't know who our customer is, we literally don't know what the word quality means. So, that's where I think founders really run into trouble and everyone's like, "Well, I'm Steve Jobs, I'm this, I have the magic taste." And it's like, "Well, first of all, do you have the years and decades of failures and experience from which that taste derives?" (00:32:55): If you do that then I'm like, "I'll give you the benefit of the doubt." And if you don't then, "Definitely don't rely on that, definitely do some experimentation. Go get those scars." But even if you have a taste, if you're completely right, what can it hurt to double check? My view was like, "Oh, let's have 10 customers look at it and have them throw up about how it's so horrible, that at least confirms that we're on the right track." (00:33:13): And then we call it establishing a baseline when we talk about innovation accounting and the metrics side of Lean Startup. Let's go find out how bad the situation is right now, so that we can then know that we improve from it. Because the thing I actually see from people who in the name of quality will wait a long time to ship a product is they ship it with really high quality and nobody uses it, and now we don't know why. Is it because our idea of quality is wrong? Is it because the value prop is fundamentally... I feel like building a high quality wrong value prop is nothing to be proud of. There's no craftsmanship in that. I once had a company that built a really beautiful product, amazing land, everything was awesome, but there was a JavaScript error where when you clicked the download button, the signup button, whatever, it didn't click. So, they launched this thing and it had 0% signups.
turns.zh:
我喜欢这个问题，因为首先，我经常被问到这个问题，而且我们真正理解这一点很重要。人们认为MVP是关于某种特定策略的。所以，MVP就像是一个最基本、最简化的产品，可能会让你的电脑崩溃，但这与MVP无关。MVP只是针对我们试图验证的假设，无论是什么假设，找到最有效的方法来验证这个假设是否正确？因此，成功测试的一部分是了解我们市场中客户的需求。现在，有趣的是人们对产品失败有着深深的恐惧——我们都有这种深深的恐惧。所以第一个答案是，你认为iOS应用商店的用户期望很高，你应该去尝试数据中心的电池备份系统购买者，或者是建造深海石油钻井机或喷气发动机的人（00:29:22）。我曾与一些公司合作，他们的标准实际上非常高，以至于iOS应用看起来都相当基础。就像，“嗯，你的应用没炸掉，但即使在这些高端行业和高风险情况下，提供用户不喜欢的产品的成本其实也不高。他们只要说不就行了，而MVP很大程度上就是为了控制犯错的风险。所以是的，我真正鼓励人们做的一件事就是去找10个客户，不是1000万，而是10个客户。让他们使用产品，并告诉你哪里糟糕。这没关系，我曾经也很生气……当我推出产品时，如果客户和我争论，他们会说，‘你这个白痴，产品没有X、Y、Z这些功能，它们太重要了。’（00:30:11）而我会说，‘你错了……’我不得不生他们的气，但后来我变得更聪明了。我会说，‘X、Y、Z，你说？’然后我会做笔记，‘哦，有意思。’有时候X、Y、Z会成为我路线图的下三个功能，而我又想和他们争论，‘我早就知道了……’最后当我们推出X、Y、Z时，他们会感到有归属感。‘哇，我就是那个告诉他要这么做的人。他本来都不会做的。’但当然，作为创业者，我们真正害怕的是，如果人们说，‘你这个白痴，没有X、Y、Z就推出产品了’，他们会说，‘你这个白痴，没有A、B、C就推出产品了’（00:30:44）。你会说，‘A、B、C是什么？’从没听说过。这才是我更常听到的反应。所以，让我们先假设期望很高的前提成立，如果我们推出一个应用但不符合人们的期望，他们就不会喜欢它。首先，这样做的后果是什么？在精益创业的早期阶段，我们必须花很多精力向人们解释产品发布和营销发布的区别。你可以向客户推出产品，而不告诉任何人你这么做了。没关系。没人会发现，也不会成为大新闻。当然，一旦你成为一家成功的大公司，那就是完全不同的问题了，现在你要在产品上印上你的企业品牌，但如果你是一家真正的初创公司，没人会在乎。所以，可以尝试一下。（00:31:29）但我认为人们没有意识到的另一件事是，MVP非常灵活。所以，如果你告诉我……当我和创业者合作时，我会说，‘听着，对不起，我们的客户
嗯……这里有个酒吧，而这个东西必须得足够出色。”我说：“太棒了，但功能肯定不能太多，否则对吧？” 他们问：“你什么意思？” 我说：“你刚刚说酒吧标准很高，所以我们最好先把一个关键功能做到那个水平，如果成功了，再考虑下一个。” 结果他们说：“哦，不不不，我要把所有功能都做到最高质量。” 我反问：“那我们测试什么？” 他们又说：“等你发现这个功能是否好用……” 看看那些失败案例，你肯定也遇到过这种情况吧。 （00:32:06）：第一版产品90%的成果都会被抛弃，无论它质量多高。这其实让我很失望。作为工程师，我最初对敏捷软件开发运动和精益创业的失望之处在于，人们承诺遵循最佳实践就能消除工作中的浪费。但如果我们做出的产品客户不想要，那才是最大的浪费，却没人能保护我们免受这种风险。所以我不在乎最初的MVP质量有多高，因为质量是由客户定义的。如果我们连客户是谁都不知道，质量这个词就毫无意义了。这就是我认为创业者容易陷入困境的地方。大家总说：“我是史蒂夫·乔布斯，我有敏锐的判断力。” 但我会问：“首先，你有多年失败的经验作为判断的基础吗？” （00:32:55）：如果你有经验，那我愿意相信你。但如果没有，就别轻信，赶紧去实验，积累经验。即便你有判断力，如果判断错了，再多检查一遍又有何妨？我的观点是：“找10个客户看看他们的反应，如果他们吐槽产品糟糕，至少说明我们方向正确。” （00:33:13）：在创新会计和精益创业的指标体系中，我们把这种摸底称为基线建立。先搞清楚当前状况有多糟糕，才能知道如何改进。那些以质量为名拖延上线产品的人，结果产品质量很高却无人问津，最后还困惑于原因。是因为我们的质量定义有误？还是因为价值主张根本有问题……我觉得构建错误的价值主张却做得很精致，实在没什么值得骄傲的。我曾遇到一家公司，他们打造了一个精美的产品，界面设计惊艳，一切都完美，但有个JavaScript错误，导致点击下载按钮或注册按钮毫无反应。产品上线后，注册量为零。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: ... click. So they launched this thing, it had 0% signups and they're like, "It's a catastrophe. We made the wrong value prop." It's like, how do you know? From one experiment you can never know. You have to be willing to do a series of experiments. Again, the logic of MVP is just, products take time to build. The best products in the world, everything takes time. It takes a month, a year. AI will mean I could build any product I want instantly. But it's not instantly, it's going to take time. (00:34:28): During that time that the product is under construction, there's going to be some moment in time when you have half the product. Just logically speaking, you first have 10%. When you have half the product, let's have customers use half the product. Well, it doesn't cost you anything extra. You had to do it. You build a natural experiment anyway. Have them use it and tell you it's only half as good or it's unusable, because it's so bad. Excellent, good. (00:34:51): The startup literature is littered with examples of people where less is more, where the crappy small thing they did turned out to be more valuable than the competitor. I'll just give you one example, one of my favorites. I come from 3D graphics and avatars and metaverse stuff, which of course, now is bad. It's one of these things goes through these hype cycles and I'm like, "Are we actually in the hype cycle or are we the drops?"
turns.zh: ……点击一下。于是他们推出了这个产品，结果注册量为零，他们就说：“这简直是灾难。我们选错了价值主张。” 但你怎么知道的？仅凭一次实验永远无法得出结论。你必须愿意进行一系列实验。再说回MVP的逻辑，产品研发需要时间。世界上最优秀的产品，哪一个不是花费数月甚至数年时间才能问世？人工智能或许能让我瞬间打造出任何想要的产品，但这绝非一蹴而就，依然需要时间。（00:34:28）在产品研发期间，往往会出现这样一个阶段：产品完成了一半。按常理来说，先推出10%的功能。当产品完成一半时，何不让用户先体验一半功能呢？反正成本不增加，而且你本来就得这么做。这样自然就能得到反馈——用户会说功能太简陋、无法使用，或者评价只是一半价值。太好了！这正是你需要的。（00:34:51）创业领域里到处都是“少即是多”的案例，比如某个劣质的小产品最终胜过竞争对手。我举个例子吧——我曾从事3D图形、虚拟形象和元宇宙相关工作，当然，现在这些领域已经过气了。技术总会经历炒作周期，我就会想：“我们现在是身处炒作周期，还是已经是被淘汰的玩家？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's trending up right now.
turns.zh: 我觉得现在这个领域正在回暖。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Are we trending up again?. It's really hard for me to keep track. Even while I was working on it, every few years it was either the future or nobody wanted to do it. I bet sales of [inaudible 00:35:25] crash, you'll probably have that cyclical thing to them. When it's hot, people read it, otherwise not. Anyway, we built a version, our first version of IMVU we built with 3D avatars in a cafe or in a scene. The avatars were all anchored in place because we didn't have the technology called inverse kinematics. We didn't have the technology that would allow an avatar to stand up and walk. When you do this 3D grab, it has to work perfectly. The feet have to actually glide along the surface and it doesn't look right. You wind up in the uncanny valley and people find it horrible. So we're like, "Can't have that." So we just have the avatar to sit there. People felt the product was claustrophobic. They would always be like, "The Sims lets me move around. Why am I stuck here in the chair?" (00:36:01): That was a very common thing in customer feedback. We were like, "We can't afford to do the expensive thing. We couldn't do it, couldn't do it." One day as a hack, as like a little demo, I was like, "Well, I'll just change it so that when you click in the scene to a different spot, we'll just stop rendering the avatar in the first place and we'll put it in the second place." We didn't even do the proper cut. The camera would zoom over there. It was really ugly. I was really embarrassed about it. I was like, let me just play around with it and see what happens. (00:36:29): We shipped it to cut and I was like, this is below the quality bar. I felt bad as the engineer. Everyone involved felt really bad, but we had committed ourselves that we're going to try to experiment with stuff. We're going to see what happens. This is before Lean Startups existed. We didn't even have the concept of MVP. We're going to try it and just see what happens. We shipped it and nothing happened. No one cared. I was like, whew. Then we used to do these daily tracking surveys. We'd just sample people and ask them what they think of the product. In the tracking surveys, people started to say that IMVU was the most advanced avatar product they'd ever used. (00:37:03): People would be like, we used to be compared to the Sims unfavorably. Now people would be like, more advanced than the Sims. I was like, what does this mean? How did we get more of, did we improve our 3D graphics design? No one could understand why they were saying that. We used to do customer interviews. Finally, a customer was like, "It's so great, man. In InView, when you want to go somewhere, you teleport. The Sims, you got to wait for the guy to get up and walk around. It's so annoying." We were just like, "Oh, my God. Embarrassing." We didn't do inverse kinematics for a really long time.
turns.zh: 我们又开始走上坡路了吗？这真的很难追踪。即使我在做项目时，每隔几年它要么是未来的趋势，要么就没人想做了。我敢打赌，[00:35:25未听清]的销售会暴跌，用户行为大概会周期性波动。天气热的时候，人们会阅读相关内容，否则就不会关注。总之，我们开发了第一个IMVU版本，里面的3D虚拟形象只能在咖啡馆或特定场景中移动。由于当时没有逆运动学技术，虚拟形象无法站起来行走。当你尝试3D互动时，动作必须完美无缺——脚步要贴合地面，但效果往往不理想，容易让人产生"不适感"，用户反馈也很糟糕。比如用户会抱怨："《模拟人生》能自由移动，为什么IMVU里的虚拟形象只能坐着？"（00:36:01）这些反馈很常见。我们当时只能说："我们负担不起昂贵的技术，实在没办法。"有一天，我临时做了个小演示：当用户在场景中点击不同位置时，虚拟形象会从当前位置消失，出现在新位置。虽然没有做完美的过渡，但效果很差，镜头扫过时画面很卡顿，我特别尴尬。当时我只想试试看效果如何。（00:36:29）我们上线后，发现用户反馈远低于预期。作为工程师，我很内疚。团队每个人都很失望，但我们坚持要尝试新技术，看看结果如何。这还是在精益创业理念出现之前，我们甚至没有最小可行产品（MVP）的概念。结果上线后毫无反响，无人问津。我松了一口气。后来我们每天做追踪调查，抽样收集用户反馈。用户突然称IMVU是他们用过最先进的虚拟形象产品。（00:37:03）以前人们总说IMVU不如《模拟人生》，现在却说IMVU比《模拟人生》更先进。我很困惑：这是怎么回事？我们是改进了3D图形设计吗？但用户说不出原因。我们常做用户访谈。终于有用户说："太棒了。InView里想去哪儿直接传送，《模拟人生》还得等角色起身走路，多烦人。"我们顿时意识到，用户是在批评《模拟人生》的交互设计。我们拖延了很久才加入逆运动学技术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that story. Something that I'm learning as you talk about MVP is that the idea of minimum is very fluid and very context specific. Essentially, the message isn't, build something low quality and simple. It's, figure out what is that minimum bar for your market and product. The message is just build as little as possible, whatever that is for you.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个故事。从你谈论MVP的过程中，我领悟到"最小可行产品"的概念非常灵活，取决于具体情境。关键不在于做低质量、简单的产品，而是要找到市场和产品的最低标准。核心在于尽可能少地开发，找到适合你的那个"最小可行产品"。

turns.speaker: Eric Ries
turns.en: Yeah, as little as necessary. It's fascinating. I'm not joking, I've worked on jet engines and robotics and cancer therapies and all kinds, I've worked on stuff anyway, and LTSE, it took us 10 years to build the MVP for LTSE. So it doesn't necessarily mean cheap low quality. It's just whatever your hypothesis is, whatever you actually believe is going to work, let's put that thing to the test. That's all I really want. When I work with companies, first time founders especially are usually very stubborn about this and they don't want to do it. It's like, "Look, you tell me what you believe. I don't have to be right and I want to just double check that you're right by however we do it." And then once people actually start to turn that idea over in their mind, they often will be like, "Well, you know..." A classic one is like, we can't sell the thing until we build the physical equipment. (00:38:48): It's like, is your product bought in a showroom where people see the physical equipment? No, they buy it from a brochure. So it's like, "Okay, well how about we send them a brochure and ask them to pre-order it?" And then it's like, what? I can't do that. I can't have a crappy brochure. It's like, who said a crappy brochure? We can build a really high quality brochure in a tiny fraction of the time it takes to build the actual machine. And then it's like, well then what are you talking about, it has really good fonts and it has pretty pictures? Maybe. What's your theory, right? You tell me what do you believe about... And they're like, "Well, actually what matters is the quality of the specifications of the equipment in the brochure." It's like, now we've got the leap of faith assumption. Let's go find out. (00:39:29): And they're like, but hold up. But we don't know what those specifications are going to be yet. It's like, well, I saw this 500 page plan over here. What do you want it to be? It's like, well, it'd be really great if customers would accept this set of performance characteristics. Well, let's go promise that because maybe they'll be like, "That's great." And I'll give you one example. I was mentioning data centers. There's a team that sold equipment and data centers. They had a serious high-end team of PhDs working on research to make the thing way more efficient and they're going to win a Nobel Prize in material sciences in order to make this product a reality. And I convinced them, instead of paying three years and $18 million, so you don't make the thing, let's go take a brochure, take it to some customers. (00:40:13): And I'll never forget, they took the thing into the brochure, they took it into customers and customers laughed them out of the room and it was nothing to do with anything they cared about. It was nothing to do with efficiency where they're like, we would never buy this. And they were like, "But you haven't even looked to page two to see how efficient it is." They were like, "We don't pay for efficiency, we build data centers. How much they cost to operate is somebody else's problem." You're like, "Oh my God." (00:40:37): That's the thing people don't appreciate, is these insights are so obvious in retrospect that everyone's convinced that it won't happen to them. When I teach students at Lean Startup, they're like, "This is so dumb." They do one case after another in business school and they're like, "Dummy, dummy, dummy, dummy, dummy, right?" They're like, "I would never make that mistake." And I'm always like, "Look, you don't have to argue with me. Just call me back when you get a job. And when you make one of these mistakes, remember we had these conversations and go read the book then." And I guess by random chance there are some people in the world that just never made a mistake. (00:41:11): The dice, you roll enough dice, somebody had the experience that dice came up double sixes every time. Okay, so there are those people and they give a lot of the advice in the world, but I don't know that it's necessarily those of us who don't have the double six luck should necessarily be following it.
turns.zh:
是的，越少越好。真是令人着迷。我没开玩笑，我曾参与过喷气发动机、机器人技术、癌症治疗等各类项目的研发。但说到LTSE，我们花了整整10年才构建出最简可行产品。所以这并不意味着产品质量低劣。关键在于，无论你的假设是什么，只要你坚信它可行，那就去验证它。这才是我真正想要的。很多初创公司，尤其是初次创业者，往往对此非常固执，死守自己的想法。比如他们会说：“看，你得先造出实体设备才能卖。”（00:38:48）我会反问：“你们的产品是在展厅里展示实体设备才卖的吗？不是啊，是通过宣传册卖的。”那又怎样？“我不能用劣质宣传册啊。”“谁说要劣质了？我们用极短时间就能做出高质量的宣传册。”然后对方会说：“那你说什么呢？字体要美观，图片要精美？”或许吧，但你的核心论点是什么？让我听听你的假设。对方会说：“关键在于宣传册里设备规格的准确性。”这时候就触及到信仰跳跃假设了。那就去验证吧。

（00:39:29）对方会说：“等等，但我们还没确定规格标准呢。”我会说：“那看看这份500页的方案吧，你希望客户接受怎样的性能指标？”对方会说：“如果客户能接受这些指标就太好了。”我举个例子。我曾接触过一个数据中心设备销售团队。他们有顶尖的博士团队致力于研发高效技术，甚至有望凭借材料科学成果获得诺贝尔奖来实现产品落地。我说服他们别花三年时间和1800万美元研发，直接拿宣传册去找客户。（00:40:13）结果令人难忘。他们带着宣传册去找客户，结果客户笑着把他们赶了出来，理由和产品本身毫无关系。他们不在乎效率，说：“我们绝不会买这个。”对方反驳：“但你们还没看第二页的效率数据呢。”更无语的是：“我们又不买效率，建数据中心是别人的事。”真是让人无语。

（00:40:37）人们总觉得这些洞见显而易见，觉得自己不会重蹈覆辙。但我在精益创业课上教学生时，他们会说：“这太蠢了。”商学院案例教学时他们也会说：“傻瓜，傻瓜，傻瓜，傻瓜，傻瓜，对吧？”他们说：“我绝不会犯那种错误。”我总说：“好吧，不用反驳我。等你找到工作了再联系我。等你成功了再来找我。”
这些错误都不是重点，记住我们之前聊过这些，回去把书读一遍吧。  
我猜世界上总有些人从不犯错。（00:41:11）比如骰子，掷足够多次骰子后，有人发现每次都掷出双六。好吧，这样的人确实存在，他们会给出很多建议，但我不确定我们这些没那么幸运每次都能掷出双六的人是否应该听从这些建议。

turns.en: This will be a really good segue to talk about pivots because again, a big part of your message is a lot of the work you're doing is just going to go to waste anyway. Why spend all this time building it? But just to put a final point on this idea of MVP, because a lot of questions came in around just like, what is an MVP? Ben Silbermann, the co-founder of Pinterest, has this quote, he didn't ask a question in our thread, but he has this quote-
turns.zh: 这将是一个很好的过渡，接下来我们来谈谈业务转型。因为同样道理，你所做的很多工作最终可能都会白费。何必花费大量时间去打造它呢？不过关于最小可行产品（MVP）的概念，我想再补充一点，因为有很多朋友问，什么是MVP？Pinterest的联合创始人本·西尔伯曼（Ben Silbermann）曾说过这样一段话，虽然他没有在我们的讨论中提问，但他的这句话值得一提——
